I doubt that. For example, comics, while very influential in popular media, were misrepresented in museums like MoMA, at least in the nineties. Major works and artists from the underground were ignored, and it took Art Spiegelman's frustration and his "Co-mix" project to change the view somewhat.

Major museums do incorporate video games (or representations of them), but they're not going to "get" the medium by themselves if designers don't communicate their ideas to them. And that assumes the institutions are receptive to communication...

This is like saying any drawing you liked wasn't art, because the act of creating it was simply a set of reproducible motions governed by a set of rules. And really, all art is exactly that. The real difference is when you look at a drawing you have a frame of reference with which to appreciate it. With software, people who do not code have no frame of reference with which to appreciate it. They see what it does when it runs, but they do not see how or why it does it the way it does.

I beg to differ. Mathematical representation and elegant solutions are definitely considered artful by many. For example, all music is mathematical. All that game art? Lighting effects? Post processing effects? Mathematical. Color selection, shading, everything. It's so common it's all around you, and hides in plain sight. Because math is the best language we have to describe our physical world, it could be considered the ultimate artistic language from which all other forms of art are derived.

Programming can also definitely be art, and is often considered such when the code manages to offer elegant solutions to complex problems. Just because you don't understand it does not mean there isn't a beauty or creativity in it for those that do.
And what is different in that aspect from an animated movie, other than interactivity?

I think interactivity is the only thing, but a powerful thing. The character's motivations and considerations literally become your own because your success in meeting goals moves the story along. It brings an extra dimension to storytelling by putting you more firmly in the role of one of the story's characters. There's also an element of choice that isn't present in most books or flim, meaning you get to decide how the story plays out to some degree. I'm not sure any of this makes it art, but I would put video game in the same category of storytelling devices that I place literature and film in.

I've been saying this for a while now: Interactive multimedia draws from several artforms.

There seems to be some debate on programming being an artform - but I assure you there's a fine difference between functional-yet-asanine code that's difficult to read and well-formatted, well-written code. Literature, for example, has an entire writing art style dedicated to the way that paragraphs are positioned in readable space - as a similar concept.

A good example of such formatting art was also a rather popular Tumblr post: http://i.imgur.com/BIDWhvy.png

Programming can definitely be an artform, but not all programming is art - just like anything can be art, but not everything is.
